analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workplace harassment and discrimination protections, bans forced arbitration, and phases out the lower minimum wage for tipped workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2024 with 23 Senate backers, the bill was sent to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul federal workplace discrimination law. Employers with 15 or more workers would have to adopt and publicize detailed anti-harassment policies and provide training, with fines for failing to comply. It would write harassment into statute as illegal under a 'totality of circumstances' test where a single incident can qualify, remove caps on compensatory and punitive damages, extend deadlines to sue, cover employers with as few as one employee, and extend protections to independent contractors, interns, and volunteers. It would also ban forced arbitration of discrimination claims, restrict nondisclosure agreements, fund legal help for low-income workers, and gradually eliminate the separate, lower minimum wage for tipped workers so they earn the full federal minimum.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination on the job, including women, people of color, LGBTQ workers, older workers, workers with disabilities, and tipped restaurant workers. Also independent contractors, interns, fellows, and volunteers, who are currently outside most federal employment discrimination law, and workers in very small businesses, since coverage would drop from 15 employees to 1.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers with 15 or more employees to adopt, disseminate, and post comprehensive nondiscrimination policies, with fines of up to $1,000 per violation and at least $5,000 for repeated or willful failures.
Directs the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to write rules requiring interactive anti-harassment training for employees and supervisors, based on research on effective training.

Writes workplace harassment into statute as an unlawful employment practice, judged on the totality of circumstances, under which a single incident can qualify and incidents are considered in the aggregate.
Removes the existing caps on compensatory and punitive damages in employment discrimination cases and extends the statutes of limitations for filing claims.
Expands coverage to employers with as few as one employee (down from 15) and extends protections to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees.
Prohibits mandatory arbitration of employment discrimination claims and restricts nondisclosure agreements, so workers can take claims to court and speak publicly.

Clarifies that discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, and pregnancy is unlawful sex discrimination, and bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a defense under Title VII.
Phases out the separate, lower cash wage for tipped workers over several years until they receive the full federal minimum wage, and confirms employees keep their tips.
Creates a national prevalence survey on workplace harassment and authorizes grants for civil legal assistance for low-income workers and for a system of state worker advocacy.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face new policy and training requirements, higher litigation exposure from uncapped damages and extended filing deadlines, and an end to forced arbitration; restaurants and other tipped-wage employers, whose labor costs would rise as the sub-minimum tipped wage is phased out; and taxpayers, who fund the new EEOC programs, surveys, and grants.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is real: covered employers must build and maintain detailed policies, disseminate them annually, and provide training, with fines starting at $1,000 per violation and $5,000 or more for repeated or willful violations.

Litigation costs would rise: the bill removes damage caps, extends filing deadlines, covers employers with a single employee, and lets a single incident count as harassment, which the businesses that would face these suits would bear as higher defense and settlement costs.

Phasing out the tipped minimum wage raises labor costs most sharply for full-service restaurants, an industry that argues the change threatens a tipping system many servers currently earn more than the minimum wage under.

The bill bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being raised as a defense under Title VII, a provision religious organizations and defenders of religious exemptions would object to on principle.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers are substantial and concrete: stronger legal standards, more time to sue, no forced arbitration, coverage for contractors and tiny employers, and a full minimum wage for tipped workers. The costs are real but ordinary: compliance work for employers, higher exposure in harassment litigation, and higher labor costs for restaurants. The strongest honest objection is that uncapped damages and broader liability standards could raise the cost of doing business, especially for small firms, and some of that cost could fall on workers through reduced hiring or hours; the bill's small-business model materials and grant programs are an attempt to soften that.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray introduced the BE HEARD in the Workplace Act on July 31, 2024, joined on introduction by 23 senators, all Democrats or allied independents.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction.
The action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House companion action, through the end of the 118th Congress.
A prior version of the BE HEARD Act was introduced in earlier Congresses and also never became law, so its core provisions remained unenacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — especially restaurants that pay the sub-minimum tipped wage and companies that rely on forced arbitration — are better off, because existing law, with its damage caps, shorter deadlines, and arbitration-friendly rules, stayed exactly as it was. Workers who would have gained stronger harassment protections gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, especially restaurants paying tipped wages

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it with 23 Senate colleagues.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: 49 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None cosponsored; the bill drew no recorded Republican support in either chamber.

against.name: Restaurant and business lobbying groups
against.what_they_did: Have publicly opposed this package's core provisions — repeal of the tipped sub-minimum wage, mandatory arbitration bans, and expanded employer liability — in past Congresses.

sides.party_line_note: The fight was entirely one-sided by party: all 23 Senate sponsors were Democrats or allied independents, not a single Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a Democratic-chaired committee without a hearing.

industries.note: The bill phases out the separate tipped minimum wage, currently $2.13 federally, until tipped workers earn the full federal minimum wage, directly raising restaurant labor costs. The industry's savings from the sub-minimum wage come at tipped workers' expense, so its interest in this bill runs against the workers it employs.

industries.industry: Employers broadly, from small businesses to large corporations
industries.note: The bill mandates policies and training with fines, extends coverage to one-employee firms and contractors, removes damages caps, extends filing deadlines, and bans forced arbitration. The cost falls on employers; the benefit is legal recourse for their workers.

industries.industry: Civil legal aid and worker advocacy organizations
industries.note: The bill authorizes federal grants for legal assistance for low-income workers and for a system of state worker advocacy, expanding funding for groups that represent workers in discrimination cases.
